About Me

Full-stack software developer with an Information Technology background and a passion for building clean, high-performance web applications and data-driven dashboards. I enjoy architecting robust backend systems and pairing them with intuitive, responsive user experiences.
summary:
I built FireBridge, an interactive dashboard that uses historical NASA FIRMS data to explore and compare active fire detections from MODIS and VIIRS. Users can locate hotspots on a map, explore daily activity in a calendar, and filter observations by date and region.

FireBridge addresses a challenge in comparing wildfire activity across satellite instruments. Differences in spatial resolution can affect how many hotspots each instrument reports. To make the comparison more consistent, FireBridge counts the unique 1 km grid cells with detections each day for each instrument. It also tests an experimental adjustment and shows how much the daily counts differ before and after adjustment on dates held back from the calculation.

The dashboard helps users see where and when fires were detected and understand how the choice of satellite instrument can affect the trends they see.
details:
FireBridge is an interactive dashboard I built as a solo participant to answer a question about satellite fire data: How much does the choice of instrument change the fire activity we see?

Explore satellite fire detections

FireBridge uses historical observations from NASA’s Fire Information for Resource Management System (FIRMS). Users can:

  • Explore MODIS and VIIRS detections on a 2D map or 3D globe.
  • Filter by region, UTC date, and instrument, then inspect individual hotspots.
  • Use the burning calendar and activity charts to see how detections change over time.
  • Export detections and comparison results as CSV files for further analysis.

Compare MODIS and VIIRS on a common grid

MODIS and VIIRS observe Earth at different spatial resolutions, which can affect how many hotspots each instrument reports. FireBridge places their detections on a shared 1 km equal-area grid and counts each detected cell once per instrument per UTC day.

The dashboard then lets users test an experimental adjustment for VIIRS. It fits the adjustment on the first 70% of dates with records from both instruments and evaluates it on the remaining dates. For Northern Australia, the mean absolute daily difference from MODIS fell from 707.7 to 106.7 detected cells across six held-out days. This result measures agreement with MODIS for that region and period. Testing other regions and seasons would help establish how well the adjustment generalizes.

Design choices and intended impact

I wanted students, educators, and anyone working with satellite fire data to see how a comparison is made and where it can be misleading. The calendar distinguishes missing records from zero detections. The comparison chart displays the original and adjusted counts together, so users can see what changed. Counting occupied grid cells also limits how much repeated detections within the same cell and day influence the comparison.

Technology

I built the dashboard with React, JavaScript, and Vite, using D3 Geo for the flat map, react-globe.gl for the globe, and Recharts for the charts. I used Python to process FIRMS records, SQLite to store and query them, and Flask to serve the data to the browser.
